events.title: Galen's Medical Writings
events.blurb: A Greek physician serving as a court doctor in a Roman imperial capital produced over 400 treatises on anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, and medical theory drawing on dissections of apes and pigs (human dissection being prohibited in the empire). His humoral-theory framework — the balance of blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile — dominated Western medicine for the next 1,400 years, long past the time when his observations had been outdated by better ones.
events.revealBlurb: c. 175 CE — Galen of Pergamon, personal physician to Emperor Marcus Aurelius. His authority was so absolute that medieval and early modern doctors would continue to insist on humoral imbalance diagnoses when dissections had shown otherwise. Harvey's circulation of the blood, 1,400 years later, began the long overthrow of Galen.

events.title: First Smallpox Vaccination
events.blurb: An English country doctor inoculated a healthy eight-year-old boy with material extracted from a milkmaid's cowpox blister, then six weeks later deliberately exposed the child to smallpox. When the boy showed no symptoms, the physician had demonstrated that a mild related disease could confer immunity against a deadly one — founding the practice of vaccination.

events.title: Koch Identifies TB Bacillus
events.blurb: A 38-year-old German physician, presenting to the Berlin Physiological Society, announced he had isolated and cultured the bacillus responsible for tuberculosis — a disease that killed roughly one in seven people in 19th-century Europe. He had developed systematic protocols — now called Koch's postulates — for identifying which microbes caused which diseases. He would identify the cholera bacillus two years later.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1882 — Robert Koch. World Tuberculosis Day is commemorated on this anniversary each year. Koch won the Nobel Prize in 1905. His attempted TB vaccine, tuberculin, was a failure — but became a useful skin test for TB exposure.

events.title: First Human Heart Transplant
events.blurb: A South African surgeon transplanted the heart of a 25-year-old accident victim into a 53-year-old grocer in a nine-hour operation at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town. The recipient survived 18 days before dying of pneumonia; the same surgical team performed a second transplant 13 days later — that patient lived 19 months.

events.title: First Heart Transplant
events.blurb: A South African surgeon led a nine-hour operation at a Cape Town hospital transplanting the heart of a 25-year-old woman, killed by a car striking her as she crossed the road to buy cake, into the chest of a 54-year-old man with severe coronary disease. The patient lived 18 days before dying of pneumonia. The surgeon instantly became internationally famous; subsequent transplant patients lived increasingly long with improved immunosuppression.
events.revealBlurb: December 3, 1967 — Christiaan Barnard at Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town. Patient: Louis Washkansky. Donor: Denise Darvall. Barnard's second patient, Philip Blaiberg, lived 19 months. The 5-year survival rate for heart transplants is now about 75 percent.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Signed
events.blurb: Fifty-five delegates meeting for four months in a Philadelphia state house, working in secret through a sweltering summer with the windows closed against spies, produced a seven-article document replacing the loose Articles of Confederation with a stronger federal framework. Thirty-nine of them signed. An 81-year-old Benjamin Franklin, who had been at nearly every session, pointed at the sun carved into George Washington's chair and said he was finally sure it was rising, not setting.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 1787 — Independence Hall, Philadelphia. Ratified June 21, 1788 after New Hampshire became the ninth state to approve. The Constitution has been amended 27 times in 235 years — less than once per decade. A different Philadelphia-era document, the Bill of Rights, followed in 1791.

events.title: Louis XVI Executed
events.blurb: A former French king, convicted by the National Convention of treason for allegedly conspiring with foreign powers against the revolution, was beheaded by a relatively new device on a Paris square as drums drowned out the opening lines of the speech he attempted to deliver from the scaffold. His wife, an Austrian-born former queen, would meet the same end nine months later. The regicide radicalized the revolution's enemies and internal fears alike.
events.revealBlurb: January 21, 1793 — Louis XVI at the Place de la Révolution (now Place de la Concorde). The National Convention had voted 361-360 for death, a margin of one. His final words were cut off by drums: "People, I die innocent..." Marie Antoinette was executed October 16, 1793.

events.title: Reign of Terror Begins
events.blurb: The French revolutionary government, governed for nearly a year by a Committee of Public Safety dominated by a 35-year-old lawyer, formalized terror as an instrument of state by enacting a law declaring "terror the order of the day." Over the following ten months, revolutionary tribunals sentenced roughly 17,000 people — noblewomen, priests, rival republicans, peasants, whoever — to the guillotine. The terror ended only when the committee turned on its own leader.
events.revealBlurb: September 5, 1793 — the phrase. Maximilien Robespierre would himself be guillotined on July 28, 1794 (9 Thermidor), bringing the terror to an abrupt end. Total executions and prison deaths during the Terror: perhaps 40,000 across the country.

events.title: Napoleon Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Corsican-born general, having ruled France as First Consul for five years, staged a coronation at the Gothic cathedral in the French capital. He had negotiated the pope's attendance; in the ceremony's most famous moment — possibly prearranged, possibly improvised — the emperor took the crown from the pope and placed it on his own head. The act was read as a message: no religious authority ratified his power.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1804 — Notre-Dame de Paris. Pope Pius VII had been brought from Rome; he sat largely passive through the ceremony. Napoleon's wife Joséphine also crowned herself empress. Jacques-Louis David's monumental painting of the coronation, finished three years later, flatters Napoleon's height among other details.

events.title: Battle of Austerlitz
events.blurb: A French army of 68,000 men, outnumbered by a combined Russian and Austrian force of 89,000, achieved what is still regarded as one of the greatest tactical victories in military history. Feigning weakness, the French commander baited his opponents into attacking his deliberately weakened right flank, then counter-attacked through the centre as the enemy's lines stretched thin. Three emperors had taken the field; two retreated; the Holy Roman Empire would formally dissolve within a year.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1805 — Napoleon's victory over Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II, on the first anniversary of his coronation. The battle is also called "the Battle of the Three Emperors." Allied casualties: ~36,000. French: ~9,000.

events.title: Marie Curie Wins Nobel Prize
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Polish-born physicist working in a converted shed in a French capital became the first woman to win the world's most prestigious scientific prize, sharing a physics award with her husband and a French colleague for their research into radioactivity. She would win it a second time, alone, in chemistry eight years later. Her notebooks are still radioactive, stored in lead-lined boxes and read only in protective clothing.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1903 — shared with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. She later became the first person, of any gender, to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her daughter Irène won a Nobel in chemistry too.

events.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
events.blurb: The United Nations General Assembly, meeting in a Paris exhibition hall, adopted a declaration of 30 articles enumerating rights that every human being was to be considered entitled to by virtue of humanity itself. The document's drafting committee, chaired by the widow of a U.S. president, had spent two years negotiating across ideological and cultural lines. No state voted against; eight abstained.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1948 — Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting committee. Adopted 48-0 with 8 abstentions (Soviet bloc, Saudi Arabia, South Africa). Translated into over 500 languages — more than any other document. December 10 is now International Human Rights Day.

events.title: First Woman Prime Minister
events.blurb: The widow of an assassinated South Asian island-nation prime minister was sworn in as his successor, becoming the first woman to lead a national government anywhere in the world. She had entered politics only after her husband's murder the previous year. She would serve three separate terms over four decades, dying in office at age 84.
events.revealBlurb: July 21, 1960 — Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka). She led a non-aligned left-of-center government; her daughter Chandrika became president 34 years later. She died on November 13, 2000, after casting her vote in a general election.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Sandra Day O'Connor Confirmed
events.blurb: A 51-year-old former state senator and state appellate judge from the American Southwest was confirmed by the U.S. Senate 99-0 as the first woman to sit on the U.S. Supreme Court, fulfilling a campaign promise the president who had nominated her made during the 1980 election. She would serve 24 years, writing decisions on affirmative action, abortion, and the disputed 2000 election.
events.revealBlurb: September 21, 1981 — confirmed; Ronald Reagan had nominated her. Her 2005 retirement was precipitated by her husband's declining health from Alzheimer's. She herself was diagnosed with dementia in 2018 and died in 2023.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Machiavelli Writes The Prince
events.blurb: An unemployed former Florentine civil servant, exiled from the city after a change of regime, wrote a compact political treatise in the form of advice to a hereditary ruler on how to acquire and maintain power. Its flat, unsentimental analysis of the uses of cruelty, deception, and popular love versus fear shocked readers and made its author's name a by-word for cynical politics. It remained unpublished until five years after his death.
events.revealBlurb: 1513 — Niccolò Machiavelli. The treatise was dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici, who almost certainly never read it. Published 1532 and promptly placed on the Papal Index of Prohibited Books in 1559. Still in print 500 years later.

events.title: The Communist Manifesto
events.blurb: A 29-year-old German-born philosopher-journalist and his 27-year-old industrialist-heir collaborator published a 23-page political pamphlet commissioned by a small London-based workers' organization. Its opening sentence — about a spectre haunting Europe — and its closing rallying cry became arguably the most politically consequential prose of the 19th century. Within three weeks, revolutions were breaking out across the continent.
events.revealBlurb: February 21, 1848 — Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. The League of the Just commissioned it. The 1848 revolutions failed; the Manifesto didn't become widely read until the 1872 edition with a new preface. By the 20th century it had shaped the political systems of a third of humanity.

events.title: Treasure Island Published
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish writer, suffering severe pulmonary illness and convalescing in the Scottish Highlands, sketched a treasure map with his 12-year-old stepson on a rainy afternoon and began improvising a story for the boy. The serialized pirate adventure novel that grew from the map — featuring a peg-legged cook, a squawking parrot, a buried fortune, and a black spot — essentially defined the iconography of piracy for the next century and a half.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 1883 — Robert Louis Stevenson. Initially serialized in the magazine Young Folks in 1881 as "The Sea Cook." The phrase "Shiver me timbers!" does not appear in the book but was popularized by its Long John Silver.

events.title: First Nobel Prize in Literature
events.blurb: A Swedish Academy of cultural grandees, following the will of the dynamite inventor who had died five years earlier leaving his fortune to fund annual prizes, selected a 62-year-old French poet as the first recipient of their literature award. Their choice was safe, genteel, and now obscure; they had passed over Leo Tolstoy, widely considered Europe's greatest living novelist. The omission has dogged the Nobel Literature Prize's reputation ever since.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1901 — Sully Prudhomme. Other early laureates passed over: Tolstoy, Chekhov, Ibsen, Zola, Mark Twain. The prize included 150,782 Swedish kronor — a substantial sum in 1901, about $3.5 million today.

events.title: Mozart's Requiem Unfinished
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Austrian composer who had been commissioned by a mysterious stranger six months earlier to compose a requiem Mass for an anonymous client died in his Vienna apartment with the work unfinished. Much of the "Dies irae" and "Lacrimosa" had been sketched only. His widow, in desperate financial circumstances, had a student complete the work to secure the remaining half of the commission fee.
events.revealBlurb: December 5, 1791 — Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, aged 35. The mysterious stranger was Count Walsegg, who meant to pass the work off as his own for his late wife. Mozart's student Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it; his contributions have been debated ever since.

events.title: The Rite of Spring Riot
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Russian composer's ballet score, depicting a pagan spring ritual with jagged rhythms, dissonant chord stacks, and primitivist choreography, premiered at a new Paris theatre and nearly caused a full-scale audience riot. Shouts, whistles, and fistfights broke out within minutes; the choreographer had to shout counts to dancers from the wings because they couldn't hear the orchestra. The piece is now considered one of the pivotal works of 20th-century music.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1913 — Igor Stravinsky and Ballets Russes at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris. Choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. The Parisian critic Carl Van Vechten reported his seat-neighbour beating rhythmically on his head with his fists in distress.

events.title: Rhapsody in Blue Premieres
events.blurb: A 25-year-old former Tin Pan Alley song-plugger's first major concert work — a one-movement concerto for piano and jazz band — premiered at a Manhattan concert hall advertised as "An Experiment in Modern Music." The piece's opening clarinet glissando, improvised in rehearsal as a joke, was left in. The concert had begun with banal novelty pieces; by the time the composer walked out to sit at the piano, the audience was dozing. He woke them up.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1924 — George Gershwin at Aeolian Hall, Manhattan. The bandleader was Paul Whiteman. The audience included Rachmaninoff, Stravinsky, Fritz Kreisler, and Sergei Rachmaninoff. United Airlines has used it as its ad music since 1987.

events.title: Strange Fruit Recorded
events.blurb: A 23-year-old African-American singer, in a Manhattan studio, recorded a song about the lynching of Black Americans that had been written by a Jewish high-school teacher from the Bronx. Her regular label refused to release it; a tiny specialty label agreed. She closed with it at every set at her Greenwich Village club, the room going dark except for a spotlight on her face, no encore permitted. The song haunted her for the rest of her short life.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 1939 — Billie Holiday, Commodore Records. Songwriter: Abel Meeropol, under the pen name Lewis Allan. Meeropol and his wife later adopted the two young sons of the executed Ethel and Julius Rosenberg.

events.title: John Lennon Shot
events.blurb: A 40-year-old former Beatle, returning to his Manhattan apartment building with his wife after a late-night recording session, was shot four times in the back at close range by a young man he had signed an autograph for earlier that afternoon. He was pronounced dead at a nearby hospital 20 minutes later. Vigils were held around the world. His wife asked that his birthday be celebrated with international moments of silence, which has since become a yearly tradition.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1980 — John Lennon at The Dakota, NYC. Shooter Mark David Chapman remains in prison, denied parole 13 times. Lennon's album "Double Fantasy" had been released three weeks earlier; it took on enormous posthumous sales.

events.title: Sputnik 1 Orbit
events.blurb: A 58-centimeter aluminum sphere carrying four radio antennas was boosted into an elliptical low Earth orbit, becoming the first artificial satellite. Its rhythmic beeping was receivable by amateur radio operators worldwide for 21 days.

events.title: Lunar Surface Landing
events.blurb: A spacecraft descended onto the Sea of Tranquility with 25 seconds of fuel remaining after the landing computer triggered five 1202 alarms caused by executive overflow. Two crew members spent 2 hours 31 minutes on the surface, collecting 21.5 kg of rock and soil and deploying a seismometer and a retroreflector array.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1969 — Apollo 11. Armstrong's first step came at 10:56 PM Eastern. The descent stage still sits on the Moon; the flag was knocked flat by the liftoff exhaust. The line was supposed to be "one small step for a man" — the transmission dropped the article, and Armstrong spent decades insisting he said it.

events.title: Grand Tour Launch
events.blurb: A Titan IIIE rocket launched a 722-kilogram probe carrying a gold-plated phonograph record with greetings in 55 languages and 116 images. Its trajectory used gravitational assists from Jupiter and Saturn to reach escape velocity.

events.title: First American Woman in Space
events.blurb: Physicist Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger as a mission specialist on STS-7, becoming the first American woman and the youngest American in space at 32. The six-day mission deployed two communications satellites and was the first shuttle flight to use a robotic arm to retrieve a free-flying satellite.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — STS-7. A reporter asked Ride before launch whether spaceflight would affect her reproductive organs; she deadpanned that no one had asked her male crewmates the same question. NASA engineers reportedly asked whether 100 tampons would be enough for the six-day flight "just to be safe." She flew again in 1984 and co-founded a science education company.

events.title: Galileo Enters Jupiter Orbit
events.blurb: NASA's Galileo spacecraft became the first to orbit an outer planet when it fired its main engine for 49 minutes to slow into Jupiter orbit. Simultaneously, a 339 kg atmospheric probe it had released five months earlier plunged into Jupiter's clouds and transmitted data for 58 minutes, surviving temperatures of 16,000 °C before being crushed by atmospheric pressure.
events.revealBlurb: December 7, 1995 — Galileo. The spacecraft's high-gain antenna failed to deploy fully in 1991, so the entire mission's data was re-routed through a low-gain antenna; engineers compressed the transmission protocols so thoroughly that Galileo sent back almost as much science as originally planned. During its eight years at Jupiter, it discovered evidence of a liquid water ocean beneath Europa's ice.

events.title: Bacon's Rebellion Burns Jamestown
events.blurb: A Virginia planter named Nathaniel Bacon rallied a mixed force of frontier settlers, indentured servants, and enslaved Africans against the colonial governor and marched on the capital, burning Jamestown to the ground. The uprising — the largest armed revolt in colonial America before the Revolution — exposed deep class and racial tensions that led planters to harden the legal distinction between Black slaves and white laborers.
events.revealBlurb: September 19, 1676 — Jamestown, Virginia. Bacon died of dysentery six weeks after burning the capital, ending the rebellion without a battle. Historians argue his multiracial army scared Virginia's elite so badly they accelerated the shift to race-based chattel slavery.

events.title: Monroe Doctrine Declared
events.blurb: An American president's annual address to Congress warned European powers against further colonization or political interference in the Western Hemisphere, a policy the United States could not yet militarily enforce but would cite for the next two centuries. The message was drafted largely by his Secretary of State, a future president himself.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1823 — James Monroe. The phrase "Monroe Doctrine" wasn't coined until 1850. Britain quietly backed the policy because it suited their own trade interests, and for decades the Royal Navy did most of the actual enforcing.

events.title: Dred Scott Decision
events.blurb: The Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that Dred Scott, an enslaved man who had lived in free states and territories, had no right to sue for his freedom — and that Congress had never possessed the authority to ban slavery from the territories, thereby invalidating the Missouri Compromise. Chief Justice Roger Taney further held that Black Americans, free or enslaved, were not citizens and had "no rights which the white man was bound to respect."
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1857 — Washington, D.C. The ruling was intended to settle the slavery question definitively; instead it inflamed the North and energized the new Republican Party. Dred Scott was freed by his original owner's family two months after the decision. He died 16 months later, a free man.

events.title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
events.blurb: At 7:55 that morning, 353 Imperial Japanese aircraft struck the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, sinking or damaging 19 ships including eight battleships and destroying 188 aircraft in under two hours. The attack killed 2,403 Americans — including 1,177 sailors and Marines aboard the USS Arizona, which exploded catastrophically and sank in nine minutes.
events.revealBlurb: December 7, 1941 — Pearl Harbor, Oahu. The USS Arizona still lies on the harbor floor; approximately 900 of her crew remain entombed inside. The declaration of war passed Congress the next day, 470–1 — the single dissenting vote was from pacifist Representative Jeannette Rankin of Montana.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education Ruling
events.blurb: A unanimous Supreme Court held that racially segregated public schools were inherently unequal and violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause, overturning the 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson doctrine of "separate but equal." The unanimous 9–0 decision, written by Chief Justice Earl Warren after months of behind-the-scenes persuasion, applied to all public schools and laid the legal foundation for desegregation across American society.
events.revealBlurb: May 17, 1954 — Washington, D.C. Chief Justice Warren had been appointed by Eisenhower, who privately thought the ruling a mistake. The lead attorney for the plaintiffs was Thurgood Marshall — who would later become the first Black justice on the very court he argued before.

events.title: SALT I Signed
events.blurb: In the ornate Vladimir Hall of the Kremlin, the leaders of the two superpowers signed the first treaty limiting strategic nuclear weapons. It froze the number of intercontinental and submarine-launched ballistic missiles on each side at then-current levels and restricted anti-missile defenses. Neither arsenal shrank, but the race for ever more warheads finally acquired guardrails.
events.revealBlurb: May 26, 1972 — Nixon and Brezhnev in Moscow. The ABM Treaty signed the same day restricted each side to two (later one) missile defense sites. The US withdrew from it in 2002 under George W. Bush.

events.title: Helsinki Accords
events.blurb: Thirty-five nations — every European country except tiny Albania, plus the U.S. and Canada — signed a sweeping final act in the Finnish capital that acknowledged post-war borders while binding signatories to respect human rights. Critics called it a sellout to Moscow. In fact, its human rights provisions gave eastern dissidents a legal framework that would undermine the regimes a decade later.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 1975 — the "Third Basket" on human rights proved subversive. Czech dissidents founded Charter 77 using its language; the Moscow Helsinki Group followed. Brezhnev didn't realize he'd just signed his system's eventual death warrant.

events.title: INF Treaty Signed
events.blurb: At a White House ceremony, the American and Soviet leaders signed a treaty requiring both sides to destroy every intermediate-range nuclear missile they possessed — the first arms-control agreement that actually cut existing weapons rather than capping their growth. Within three years, 2,692 missiles had been verifiably dismantled.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1987 — Reagan and Gorbachev. Both Pershing IIs and SS-20s were eliminated. The treaty was abandoned in 2019 after mutual accusations of cheating, ending a 32-year cornerstone of European security.

events.title: German Reunification
events.blurb: On a crisp autumn evening, a huge black, red, and gold flag was raised in front of the Reichstag building as the East German state ceased to exist and its 16 million citizens became part of the unified federal republic. Forty-five years of partition, imposed by four occupying armies, ended at the stroke of midnight. Crowds sang the national anthem for the first time as one country.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1990 — the date is now German Unity Day. The integration cost West Germany over €2 trillion over three decades. Many eastern cities still empty out; many western taxpayers still grumble about the "solidarity surcharge."

events.title: Soviet Union Dissolves
events.blurb: In a televised resignation speech, the last leader of a superpower announced the end of his office and, by implication, the end of the 69-year-old multinational state he had led for six and a half years. The hammer-and-sickle flag was lowered above the Kremlin for the final time and replaced with the Russian tricolor. Fifteen newly independent countries inherited the ruins.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1991 — Mikhail Gorbachev's resignation. The USSR formally ceased to exist the next day. Gorbachev lived another 31 years, mostly ignored at home and celebrated abroad, occasionally appearing in Pizza Hut and Louis Vuitton ads.

events.title: The Mother of All Demos
events.blurb: A 43-year-old Stanford Research Institute engineer delivered a 90-minute live demonstration to 1,000 conference attendees in San Francisco that showcased a computing system combining the mouse, windowing interface, hypertext links, real-time text editing, screen sharing, and video conferencing — all two decades before any of these became available on a commercial computer. The audience sat in stunned silence.
events.revealBlurb: December 9, 1968 — Douglas Engelbart at the Fall Joint Computer Conference. His live video link from his Menlo Park lab used four microwave stations. Xerox PARC, founded in 1970, hired many of his team; Apple later hired Xerox's. Engelbart's lab invented it all first.

events.title: Sony Walkman Released
events.blurb: A Japanese electronics company released a portable personal cassette player, weighing 390 grams, with headphones instead of a speaker. It had no record function — unusual for a cassette player — and its CEO personally insisted on this as a way of encouraging private, solitary music consumption. The device created an entirely new product category and pulled portable listening out of the car radio and boombox and into the individual's pocket for the next quarter-century.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 1979 — Sony TPS-L2. Co-founder Masaru Ibuka had wanted something compact to enjoy opera on long flights. The original name in Japan was "Walkman"; in the US, "Soundabout"; in the UK, "Stowaway." "Walkman" eventually won out globally.

events.title: iMac Released
events.blurb: A California computer company, newly returned to profitability under a recently returned co-founder, released an all-in-one desktop machine housed in a translucent Bondi-blue plastic case, with no floppy drive, a built-in USB port, and a round puck of a mouse. Industrial designer Jonathan Ive had led the design. The machine was derided on spec by some industry press; it sold over 800,000 units in the first five months and rescued the company's consumer business.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1998 — Apple iMac G3, designed by Jonathan Ive under Steve Jobs. The "i" prefix, coined by copywriter Ken Segall, would carry over to iPod, iPhone, iPad, iCloud. The translucent plastic shell was revolutionary for its time.

events.title: iPod Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a white portable music player with a 5 GB hard drive — "1,000 songs in your pocket," according to its co-founder's introduction — and a scrollwheel for navigation. The industry press was unimpressed; smaller MP3 players already existed. Over the next decade, the iPod and its derivatives would sell over 400 million units, reshape the music industry, and serve as a forerunner and technological foundation for the iPhone.
events.revealBlurb: October 23, 2001 — Apple iPod. Steve Jobs introduced it at a small press event, not to a large keynote crowd. Initial reviews focused on how it was Mac-only; the 2003 Windows version opened the floodgates.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: Super Mario Bros. Released in Japan
events.blurb: A moustachioed Italian plumber leaping over mushrooms and sliding down pipes became the defining character of interactive entertainment. The game shipped as a pack-in with the Nintendo Entertainment System and single-handedly revived an industry that had collapsed two years earlier under the weight of its own shovelware.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 1985 — Super Mario Bros. launched for Nintendo's Famicom in Japan. It sold over 40 million copies, a record that stood until Wii Sports in 2009. Designer Shigeru Miyamoto built the entire world around the mechanic of a running jump.

events.title: Doom Uploaded to the Internet
events.blurb: At midnight, id Software attempted to upload its new game to a university FTP server. So many people were already waiting that the network collapsed. When the file finally went live, 10,000 simultaneous downloads crashed it again. Doom popularised the first-person shooter genre, the shareware distribution model, online multiplayer, user-generated mods, and the moral panic about video game violence — all within a few months.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1993 — id Software uploaded Doom to an FTP server at the University of Wisconsin–Madison after working 30 consecutive hours. The game sold over 2 million retail copies and was installed on an estimated 10 million PCs via shareware by 1995.

events.title: The Sims Released
events.blurb: A game in which you build a house and manage the life of a simulated person — feeding them, making them use the bathroom, watching them catch fire if left unattended too long — became the best-selling PC game of the year, and then 2001, and then the best-selling PC game of all time. More than half its players were women, permanently disproving every assumption the games industry held about its audience.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2000 — Maxis and EA released The Sims for Windows. It sold 1.77 million copies in North America in its first year. The Sims overtook Myst to become the best-selling PC game ever in 2002. The franchise has sold over 70 million copies.

events.title: League of Legends Launches
events.blurb: A free-to-play adaptation of a Warcraft III fan modification launched quietly and grew into the most-played PC game on Earth. At its peak over 100 million accounts had been registered, and its annual World Championship filled football stadiums and drew broadcast audiences that dwarfed traditional sporting events. It invented a new genre name — MOBA — and made esports a career path.
events.revealBlurb: October 27, 2009 — Riot Games released League of Legends in North America. It was free-to-play from day one, monetised through cosmetic skins. The 2019 World Championship Finals drew over 100 million unique viewers. Riot was acquired by Tencent in 2011.

events.title: Fortnite Battle Royale Mode Launches
events.blurb: Epic released a free-to-play mode in which 100 players parachuted onto an island and fought until one survived, funded entirely by cosmetic purchases. Within two months it had more players than any game in history. It didn't invent the battle royale genre, but it perfected the business model — and convinced the rest of the industry that free-to-play with optional cosmetics was the future.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 2017 — Fortnite Battle Royale launched free on PC, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One. Within two months it had 45 million players. The game's in-game concerts — including Travis Scott's 2020 event with 12.3 million simultaneous viewers — redefined live entertainment.

events.title: Hippocratic Oath Composed
events.blurb: Greek medical writers associated with a physician teaching on an Aegean island composed a short ethical oath addressed to Apollo and Asclepius, binding physicians to care for their patients, respect their teachers, preserve patient confidences, and do no harm. The document is arguably the oldest surviving code of professional ethics. Modern versions, substantially modified, are still sworn by many medical-school graduates.
events.revealBlurb: c. 400 BCE — attributed to Hippocrates of Kos, though probably composed by his students or school. The modern "first, do no harm" is actually not in the original Greek text; it appears later in Hippocrates' Epidemics. The oath still shows up at white-coat ceremonies.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: First Test-Tube Baby
events.blurb: A baby girl was delivered by caesarean section at a Lancashire hospital — the first human born via in vitro fertilization. Her conception had involved an egg retrieved from her mother, fertilized in a laboratory dish, and implanted in the uterus nine years after the research team had first proposed the technique. The birth prompted intense ethical debate and religious protest. By 2020, about 1 percent of the world's babies were born via IVF.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1978 — Louise Brown at Oldham General Hospital. Pioneers: Robert Edwards, Patrick Steptoe, Jean Purdy. Edwards won the Nobel Prize in 2010 at age 85; Steptoe and Purdy had died. Brown herself had a second son born naturally in 2013.

events.title: HPV Vaccine Approved
events.blurb: A quadrivalent vaccine against human papillomavirus — the cause of virtually all cervical cancers and several other cancers — received approval from the US Food and Drug Administration for girls and women aged 9-26. The vaccine, developed initially by an Australian immunologist and colleagues, had been shown in clinical trials to be nearly 100 percent effective at preventing infection by the viral strains responsible for 70 percent of cervical cancer. Cervical cancer incidence began declining visibly within a decade.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 2006 — Gardasil (Merck), developed from research by Ian Frazer and Jian Zhou. Australia's school-based vaccination program has since essentially eliminated cervical-cancer-causing HPV strains from young women there. The vaccine's politically fraught rollout in the US slowed uptake in the 2010s.

events.title: First COVID-19 Vaccine Authorized
events.blurb: The US Food and Drug Administration issued an emergency use authorization for a novel mRNA-based vaccine against SARS-CoV-2, developed in less than a year from the publication of the virus's genetic sequence — a timescale previously thought impossible for a vaccine. The mRNA technology, which instructs the body's own cells to produce viral spike protein that the immune system then learns to recognize, had been in development for decades but had never been used in a licensed vaccine.
events.revealBlurb: December 11, 2020 — Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine. Moderna's similar mRNA vaccine followed December 18. Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, whose basic mRNA research had been neglected for years, won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Over 13 billion COVID vaccine doses were administered globally in the first three years.

events.title: Great Exhibition Opens
events.blurb: Queen Victoria opened a five-month international exhibition of industrial and artistic products housed in a vast prefabricated iron-and-glass structure in Hyde Park — the building nicknamed the "Crystal Palace." 14,000 exhibitors from 25 countries displayed 100,000 exhibits; six million visitors paid admission. The exhibition's organizer, Prince Albert, had intended it as both a celebration of industrial progress and a showcase for the superiority of free trade. It made a healthy profit, used to found London museums.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1851 — Prince Albert's Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations. Designer Joseph Paxton, a gardener turned architect, had designed the building in a single afternoon on a sheet of blotting paper. The profit funded the Victoria and Albert, Science, and Natural History museums.

events.title: Edison's Practical Lightbulb
events.blurb: After 14 months of systematic experimentation with thousands of possible filament materials — and many previous lightbulb designs by other inventors — an American inventor's laboratory team achieved a 40-hour burn using a carbonized cotton-thread filament in an evacuated glass bulb. The achievement's significance was not inventing the lightbulb itself (which had existed in various forms for decades) but making one that burned long enough to be commercially viable.
events.revealBlurb: October 21, 1879 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. His 1880 improved version used a bamboo filament and burned 1,200 hours. Edison's real genius was less invention than the systematic industrial R&D lab he created — the template for every modern corporate research operation.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Marconi's Transatlantic Radio
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Italian-Irish electrical engineer and his assistants received, from a 300-metre wire antenna held aloft by a kite on a Newfoundland cliff, three short pulses — the letter S in Morse code — transmitted from a 25-kilowatt spark-gap generator in Cornwall, 3,400 kilometres away. The reception was brief, weak, and disputed by physicists who believed radio waves travelled only in straight lines and could not follow Earth's curvature. Subsequent experiments settled the argument.
events.revealBlurb: December 12, 1901 — Guglielmo Marconi at Signal Hill, St. John's, Newfoundland, receiving from Poldhu, Cornwall. He won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics. The ionosphere's existence, which enables long-wave radio propagation around the planet, was not understood until the 1920s.

events.title: First Moving Assembly Line
events.blurb: A Detroit automobile company introduced a moving chassis-assembly line at its Highland Park plant, cutting the time needed to assemble a car from 12 hours to 93 minutes. The innovation — borrowed in part from Chicago meatpacking "disassembly" lines — let the company slash prices and dramatically increase production. The line's relentless pace was hated by workers; the company had to double wages the following year to keep them on the job.
events.revealBlurb: December 1, 1913 — Ford Motor Company, Highland Park plant. The $5/day wage (equivalent to about $140/day today) followed on January 5, 1914. Workers' turnover at the plant dropped from 370 percent annually to near zero. The wage offer drew applicants by the thousands; police had to turn away crowds in a near-riot.

events.title: Brunelleschi's Dome Completed
events.blurb: A Florentine goldsmith turned architect completed, after 16 years of work without scaffolding, a vast octagonal dome over the crossing of a century-old cathedral. The double-shelled design, assembled with four million bricks in a self-supporting herringbone pattern, spanned 42 metres — wider than any dome built since Roman antiquity. The cathedral had stood domeless for over a century, waiting for someone to figure out how.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1436 — consecrated. Filippo Brunelleschi at Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence. He refused to leave blueprints, fearing competitors would steal the ideas. Part of the technique was rediscovered only in the 20th century through forensic study of the bricks.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Magellan Sets Sail
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Portuguese-born captain, working for the Spanish crown because his own king had rejected his project, left a Sevillian port with five small ships and 270 men on a westward voyage to the spice-rich islands of Southeast Asia. He was convinced a sea passage through the Americas existed. He would find it — and a strait at the continent's southern tip is now named after him — but he would never see its other end.
events.revealBlurb: September 20, 1519 — Ferdinand Magellan. He was killed on the Philippine island of Mactan on April 27, 1521 by troops of the local chief Lapu-Lapu. One of his five ships completed the first circumnavigation — returning with 18 survivors and a load of cloves that covered the entire expedition's costs.

events.title: Council of Trent Opens
events.blurb: A general council of the Catholic Church, convened by the pope at a cathedral city in the Alpine foothills of northern Italy, opened with the task of responding to the Protestant Reformation. It met in three phases over 18 years, affirmed virtually every doctrine Protestants had rejected, standardized the Latin Mass, required bishops to reside in their dioceses, and launched the Counter-Reformation. Its decisions shaped Catholic practice for four centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 13, 1545 — opening of the Council of Trent. Its reforms hardened the Catholic/Protestant split rather than healing it. The Tridentine Latin Mass, established here, remained the standard form until the Second Vatican Council in 1965.

events.title: Galileo's Telescope Observations
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Paduan university mathematics professor, having improved the magnification of a newly invented Dutch optical toy from 3x to 30x, pointed his telescope at the night sky. Over the following months he observed craters on the moon, four previously unknown moons circling Jupiter, phases of Venus, and individual stars resolvable in the milky white band of the Milky Way. His findings, published in a short Latin book, transformed astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: January 7, 1610 — Galileo Galilei observed Jupiter's moons from Padua. His book "Sidereus Nuncius" (The Starry Messenger) was rushed into print in March. The phases of Venus, observed later that year, were decisive evidence against the Ptolemaic earth-centered model.

events.title: Awaara Released
events.blurb: A Raj Kapoor crime drama about a judge's illegitimate son — playing on the 1940s debate over heredity versus environment — became India's highest-grossing domestic release of the year and then, when dubbed and released abroad three years later, drew 64 million viewers in the Soviet Union alone, a record for any foreign film in that market. Its theme song became a street-singing anthem across Eurasia.
events.revealBlurb: December 14, 1951 — Raj Kapoor directed and starred. The song "Awaara Hoon" was so popular in the USSR, Turkey, and China that Soviet children grew up singing it phonetically in Hindi. Kapoor was reportedly stopped in Moscow streets for autographs.

events.title: Film and Television Institute of India Founded
events.blurb: A national school for cinema craft, established on the former premises of a shuttered studio whose golden era had passed, began training directors, cinematographers, and sound engineers in a new medium that independent India wanted to shape on its own terms. Its graduates would go on to redefine the aesthetic vocabulary of both art-house and popular Indian filmmaking.
events.revealBlurb: 1960, Pune. Built inside the Prabhat Film Company compound. Satyajit Ray advised on its curriculum. Early graduates include Shyam Benegal, Adoor Gopalakrishnan, Mrinal Sen, Girish Karnad — essentially the entire generation that invented Indian parallel cinema.

events.title: Deewaar Released
events.blurb: A story of two brothers who grow up in identical poverty but choose radically different paths — one becomes a dock smuggler, the other a policeman — gave Indian cinema one of its defining confrontation scenes. Its dialogue was so tightly constructed that screenwriters Salim-Javed became as famous as directors, the first time a writing duo achieved superstar status in Bollywood.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1975 — directed by Yash Chopra. Amitabh Bachchan's character has "mere paas maa hai" spoken against him, not by him — the misattribution became India's most-repeated film misquote. Director's first choices were Dev Anand and Rajesh Khanna; both were unavailable.

events.title: Taare Zameen Par Released
events.blurb: A film about an eight-year-old with undiagnosed dyslexia shipped off to boarding school for failing every subject — told largely from the child's hallucinatory perspective — earned ₹98 crore worldwide and prompted school boards across India to introduce dyslexia screening. Its child lead, discovered through an open casting call, had never acted before.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2007 — Aamir Khan's directorial debut, having taken over from Amole Gupte mid-production. Darsheel Safary, then 9, auditioned among 1,000 children. The film catalysed new Indian legislation on learning disability accommodation in schools. Khan dedicated the film to every child who had been misunderstood.

events.title: 3 Idiots Released
events.blurb: A comedy about three engineering students raging against rote-learning and parental ambition broke every domestic box-office record on its first day, earned over ₹460 crore worldwide, and set the US box-office record for an Indian film with $4.8 million from 120 American theatres. Its two-word catchphrase — "Aal izz well" — entered everyday Indian speech almost immediately.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 2009 — directed by Rajkumar Hirani, loosely based on Chetan Bhagat's novel Five Point Someone. Aamir Khan, then 44, played a college student. The film triggered a genuine policy conversation about India's education system and student mental health.

events.title: The Jazz Singer Released
events.blurb: A Warner Brothers feature film about a cantor's son who runs away to become a vaudeville singer premiered at a Times Square theatre as the first full-length motion picture with synchronized recorded dialogue. The star, in blackface for most of the film, delivered the industry's first-ever spoken movie line: "Wait a minute, wait a minute. You ain't heard nothin' yet!" Within three years almost every Hollywood film was a talkie.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1927 — Al Jolson at the Warners' Theatre, NYC. The film's sound system, Vitaphone, used synchronized phonograph records rather than optical audio. The silent era ended astonishingly fast; by 1930 the major Hollywood studios had written off the previous decade's technology.

events.title: Gone with the Wind Premieres
events.blurb: A Hollywood producer premiered a 221-minute Civil War epic at a Southern U.S. theatre, 18 months of casting speculation and three and a half hours of runtime in the making. Parade crowds lined the streets; the event was broadcast on national radio. The film swept the Oscars and set a box-office record that, inflation-adjusted, has never been surpassed. Its racial politics — a romanticized view of the antebellum South and of slavery — have made its legacy contested.
events.revealBlurb: December 15, 1939 — Loew's Grand Theatre, Atlanta. Hattie McDaniel won Best Supporting Actress for her role as Mammy, the first African-American to win an Oscar. She was segregated to a side table at the ceremony and barred from the premiere itself.

events.title: Titanic Released
events.blurb: A Canadian director released a 195-minute romantic epic about a fictional couple aboard the 1912 maiden voyage of the British ocean liner. The production had been the most expensive in Hollywood history, its budget having doubled during filming; industry wags predicted financial disaster. The film ran in theatres for ten months, won 11 Oscars, and became the first film to gross over a billion dollars. Its director famously shouted "I'm king of the world" from the podium.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1997 — James Cameron, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet. It grossed $2.2 billion; Cameron's subsequent "Avatar" beat it 12 years later, also directed by him. Celine Dion's "My Heart Will Go On" spent three weeks at #1.

events.title: The Fellowship of the Ring Released
events.blurb: A New Zealand director released the first of three films shot simultaneously in his homeland adapting a mid-20th-century English fantasy novel. The ensemble cast and landscape cinematography, the 5,000 days of digital effects by a Wellington-based studio, and the willingness to treat the fantasy material completely seriously pulled the genre from ghetto to respectability. The trilogy's final instalment would win 11 Oscars.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 2001 — Peter Jackson. The three films were shot over 438 days in New Zealand. Jackson's Weta Workshop became a world-leading effects house. The author's son Christopher Tolkien openly disliked the adaptations but inherited the royalty checks regardless.

events.title: Spirited Away Wins Oscar
events.blurb: A Japanese animated film about a 10-year-old girl's adventure in a bathhouse for spirits won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, an unprecedented achievement for an Asian work in the category. The film's director, then 62, had been making animated features for decades, but most American audiences had never heard of him or his studio. The Oscar made the director a household name and put his studio's catalog on every arthouse wishlist.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2003 — Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli's film won Best Animated Feature. Miyazaki did not attend the ceremony in protest of the Iraq War. "Spirited Away" remains Japan's highest-grossing film and grossed over $395 million worldwide.

events.title: Jamestown Colony Founded
events.blurb: English settlers dispatched by the Virginia Company came ashore on a low, marshy peninsula in the tidewater and drove stakes for the first permanent English settlement in the territory that would become the United States. Of the roughly 104 men and boys who arrived, fewer than 40 survived their first year, undone by brackish drinking water, starvation, and disease.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1607 — Virginia. The site was chosen partly because its deep water let ships dock without anchors — and partly because it looked easy to defend. It was also mosquito-ridden and had no fresh water. Within nine months, roughly 65% of the colonists were dead.

events.title: Boston Tea Party
events.blurb: That winter night, some 116 colonists disguised as Mohawk warriors boarded three ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the water, destroying approximately £10,000 worth of merchandise. The targeted destruction was a direct protest against the Tea Act, which granted the company a monopoly while taxing colonial consumers.
events.revealBlurb: December 16, 1773 — Boston Harbor. Not a single participant was ever prosecuted. Britain's furious response — the Coercive Acts, which colonists renamed the Intolerable Acts — did more to unify colonial resistance than the tea party itself. The name "Boston Tea Party" wasn't coined until decades later.

events.title: Marbury v. Madison: Judicial Review Established
events.blurb: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the unanimous Supreme Court opinion in a case about a disputed judicial appointment, using it to announce that federal courts possessed the power to strike down laws they found incompatible with the Constitution — a power the Constitution itself does not explicitly mention. The ruling transformed the Supreme Court from the weakest branch of government into an equal arbiter of constitutional meaning.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1803 — Washington, D.C. Marshall's genius was ruling against Marbury (who wanted his commission) so Jefferson couldn't refuse to comply, while simultaneously claiming the Court's enormous new power. Jefferson privately hated the decision but was trapped. The ruling wasn't used to strike down another law for 54 more years.

events.title: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg Executed
events.blurb: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed by electric chair at Sing Sing Prison, having been convicted of passing atomic bomb design secrets to the Soviet Union — making them the only American civilians executed for espionage during the Cold War. Their case divided the nation, with their guilt debated in editorial pages, union halls, and diplomatic cables around the world.
events.revealBlurb: June 19, 1953 — Ossining, New York. Ethel Rosenberg required three jolts of electricity before she died; Julius was pronounced dead after the first. Subsequent release of Soviet archives confirmed Julius was a spy; historians still debate the extent of Ethel's involvement.

events.title: House Impeaches President Clinton
events.blurb: The House of Representatives voted to impeach President Bill Clinton on the 19th of that month, on charges of perjury before a grand jury (228–206) and obstruction of justice (221–212) arising from his false testimony about a sexual relationship with White House intern Monica Lewinsky. Clinton became only the second U.S. president ever to be impeached; the Senate acquitted him on both articles the following February.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1998 — U.S. Capitol. The vote occurred while U.S. warplanes were bombing Iraq (Operation Desert Fox), which the White House denied was timed to distract from the impeachment. House Speaker-designate Bob Livingston resigned that same day. Clinton's approval rating on the day of his impeachment was 73%.

events.title: Cabbage Patch Kids Craze
events.blurb: Mass-marketed soft dolls with distinctive rotund faces, each shipped with an individual "birth certificate" and name, became the must-have Christmas gift of the holiday shopping season in the United States. Retail stampedes, fights, and injuries were reported as parents competed to buy the limited supplies of the dolls — Coleco had grossly underestimated demand. Adjusted for population, Cabbage Patch Kids may have sold more units in their peak years than any toy ever.
events.revealBlurb: December 1983 — Coleco. Xavier Roberts had been selling hand-sewn versions ("Little People") at craft fairs for years before the mass-market deal. Riots and fights occurred at multiple US stores; Coleco sold about 3 million dolls in 1983 and 20 million by the end of 1984.

events.title: Madonna's "Like a Prayer" Video
events.blurb: The music video for a 30-year-old singer's new single, featuring burning crosses, stigmata, and the singer kissing a Black saint statue coming to life, premiered during a Pepsi commercial at the start of a television special paid for by the soft-drink company. The Vatican condemned the video as blasphemous; conservative Christian groups organized boycotts; Pepsi paid the singer $5 million to sever their sponsorship deal. Her album sold 15 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1989 — the Pepsi commercial; the full video premiered on MTV March 3. Director Mary Lambert. The controversy gave Madonna an estimated $5 million for the Pepsi deal plus enormous free publicity; she kept the money. The album "Like a Prayer" remains her best-reviewed.

events.title: The Simpsons Premieres
events.blurb: A half-hour animated primetime sitcom about a dysfunctional yellow-skinned family in the fictional American town of Springfield premiered as a Christmas special on a fledgling US television network. The show's acerbic satire, cartoon slapstick, and unprecedented crossover appeal — with children and adults watching together — established animation as a legitimate prime-time format. It is still in production three and a half decades later, the longest-running American scripted prime-time TV series.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1989 — the Christmas special "Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire" on the Fox network. Created by Matt Groening from shorts he had been making for The Tracey Ullman Show since 1987. The family was named after Groening's own family except Bart, an anagram of "brat."

events.title: Titanic Premieres in the US
events.blurb: A three-hour romantic drama set aboard a doomed ocean liner's maiden voyage opened in American cinemas after a $200 million production budget — then the most expensive film ever made. It held the record as the highest-grossing film in history for twelve years and was the first to earn $1 billion and later $2 billion worldwide.

events.title: South Park Premieres
events.blurb: An animated half-hour adult-comedy series about four foul-mouthed 8-year-old boys in a small Colorado mountain town premiered on the Comedy Central cable network. The deliberately crude cut-paper animation style and its topical-to-the-minute production timeline (each episode was produced in a week rather than the months typical for animation) gave it a reactive speed no other animated show could match. It would remain in production for over 25 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1997 — created by Trey Parker and Matt Stone. Their earlier Christmas short, "The Spirit of Christmas," had circulated as a VHS among Hollywood executives in 1995. The show's 1999 feature film nearly received an NC-17 rating; the MPAA gave it R after the creators submitted it six times.

events.title: Battleship Potemkin Released
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Soviet director released a 75-minute silent film dramatizing a 1905 mutiny on a Russian imperial battleship. Its centerpiece, a massacre sequence on a flight of stone stairs in the Black Sea port city of Odessa, introduced a style of rapid associative editing that reshaped 20th-century cinema. A baby's pram bounces downward through the gunfire in a shot that has been quoted by dozens of later filmmakers.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 1925 — Sergei Eisenstein. The Odessa Steps massacre is fictional; no such event occurred in 1905. The pram shot has been homaged in The Untouchables, Brazil, and The Simpsons. Joseph Goebbels reportedly called the film "a marvelous film without equal."

events.title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
events.blurb: Walt Disney's first full-length animated feature premiered at a Los Angeles theatre — a project industry insiders had dismissed throughout its three-year production as "Disney's folly" that would bankrupt the studio. 800 artists had drawn 250,000 individual cel frames. The 83-minute film made nearly $8 million in its first release on a budget of $1.5 million, rescued the studio's finances, and launched the modern feature-animation industry.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 1937 — Carthay Circle Theatre, Los Angeles. Disney received an honorary Oscar consisting of one regular-sized statuette and seven miniature ones, presented by Shirley Temple. Adjusted for inflation, the film is still among the top-grossing of all time.

events.title: Seven Samurai Released
events.blurb: A Japanese director released a 207-minute epic about a defenseless farming village that hires seven masterless samurai to protect it from annual bandit raids. The film's action-adventure template — a diverse team of skilled specialists assembled for a dangerous mission — has been imitated in countless subsequent movies across every genre. One of its rainy climactic battles required 18 weeks of shooting and 500 tons of supplemental water.
events.revealBlurb: April 26, 1954 — Akira Kurosawa, starring Toshiro Mifune. The film was remade by Hollywood six years later as "The Magnificent Seven." The 2016 Marvel film "The Avengers" has been called, by its own director, a direct descendant.

events.title: Apocalypse Now Released
events.blurb: An American director released a 153-minute film loosely adapting Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" to the context of the Vietnam War, shot over 238 days in the Philippines through a typhoon that destroyed much of the set, an on-set heart attack for his leading man, and a drug-fueled spiral for his support cast. He screened a rough cut at Cannes with the warning: "My film is not about Vietnam. My film is Vietnam."
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1979 — Francis Ford Coppola, starring Martin Sheen and Marlon Brando. The documentary "Hearts of Darkness" chronicles the production's mayhem. Brando arrived on set overweight and unprepared; Coppola had to shoot him in shadow from the shoulders up.

events.title: Avatar Released
events.blurb: A Canadian director returning to live-action feature filmmaking after a 12-year absence released a 162-minute science-fiction epic set on a moon orbiting a distant gas giant, shot with a new custom-built 3D camera system and populated by performance-captured 3-metre-tall blue aliens. The film's production had taken four years after the technology he needed had taken another decade. It became the highest-grossing film of all time and held the title for ten years.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2009 — James Cameron. The film grossed $2.9 billion on its initial run, briefly lost the title to Avengers: Endgame, then retook it with a 2021 re-release in China. Cameron had first written the treatment in 1994.

events.title: Newton's Principia Published
events.blurb: A three-volume work laid out universal laws of motion and gravitation in mathematical form, explaining why apples fall and why planets orbit in ellipses with a single unified framework. The laws held that every mass in the universe attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their distance.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1687 — Edmond Halley paid for the printing out of his own pocket after the Royal Society spent its book budget on a history of fishes. Newton later said a dispute over priority with Robert Hooke was the reason he almost withheld the whole thing.

events.title: Oxygen Named and Combustion Explained
events.blurb: A French chemist named a newly isolated gas "oxygen" and demonstrated through careful weight measurements that combustion was not the release of a mysterious substance called phlogiston, but rather the combination of a material with this gas from the air. By showing that reactions in sealed systems conserved total mass, the work established quantitative chemistry as a discipline.
events.revealBlurb: 1778–1779 — Antoine Lavoisier's wife Marie-Anne translated English chemistry papers for him, drew the laboratory illustrations in his textbook, and helped design experiments. She is now recognised as an essential scientific collaborator, though her contributions went unacknowledged for two centuries. Lavoisier was guillotined in 1794; a judge reportedly said "the Republic has no need of scientists."

events.title: Radium Announced
events.blurb: A husband-and-wife chemistry team announced the isolation of a new radioactive element extracted from several tonnes of pitchblende ore, reporting it was approximately 900 times more radioactive than uranium. The woman researcher would go on to become the first person to win two Nobel Prizes in different scientific disciplines.

events.title: Radium Discovered
events.blurb: After months of processing tonnes of uranium ore residue in a leaky shed, two researchers announced the existence of a second highly radioactive element — far more active per gram than uranium alone. The new element glowed faintly in the dark, making the laboratory notebooks radioactive enough to be hazardous even today. The work established radioactivity as an atomic property rather than a chemical reaction.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 1898 — Marie and Pierre Curie's notebooks are still too radioactive to handle without protection; researchers must sign a waiver to view them in the French national library. Marie Curie remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911).

events.title: Uncertainty Principle Formulated
events.blurb: A paper established that it is fundamentally impossible to know both the exact position and exact momentum of a quantum particle simultaneously — the more precisely one is measured, the less precisely the other can be known, not because of measurement limitations but as a feature of nature itself. The principle implied that determinism at the subatomic scale was not merely unknown but unknowable.
events.revealBlurb: March 1927 — Werner Heisenberg derived the uncertainty principle while working alone in Copenhagen, having sent Niels Bohr on vacation. Bohr returned and disputed the physical interpretation, sparking weeks of argument. Albert Einstein spent years devising thought experiments to disprove the principle; Bohr refuted each one.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racially segregated public schools are "inherently unequal" and therefore unconstitutional, overturning the 58-year-old "separate but equal" doctrine. The narrow ruling on schools would expand over the next decade to strike down segregation in parks, beaches, swimming pools, and every other public facility.
events.revealBlurb: May 17, 1954 — Chief Justice Earl Warren assembled a 9-0 majority despite internal resistance. Enforcement took years; Arkansas governors called out the national guard to bar Black students, and some counties closed their schools entirely rather than integrate.

events.title: Montgomery Bus Boycott Ends
events.blurb: After 381 days of Black residents walking, carpooling, and riding Black-owned taxis rather than boarding segregated city buses, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a lower-court ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The next morning, Martin Luther King Jr. and Rosa Parks boarded an integrated bus in the front seats. The boycott had nearly bankrupted the transit system.
events.revealBlurb: December 20, 1956 — Martin Luther King rose to national prominence via the boycott. The organizing bureau ran car-pool lots that transported 30,000 people a day. Many Black women walked miles to work for over a year. "My feet is tired," one said famously, "but my soul is rested."

events.title: Greensboro Sit-Ins
events.blurb: Four Black college freshmen sat down at the segregated lunch counter of a downtown variety store in a North Carolina city and politely ordered coffee. When refused service, they stayed seated until closing. They returned the next day with more students. Within two months, similar sit-ins had spread to 55 cities in 13 states, and the variety-store chain desegregated its counters.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 1960 — Woolworth's lunch counter, Greensboro. The original four were students at North Carolina A&T State University: Ezell Blair, Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil, David Richmond. Part of the counter is now in the Smithsonian.

events.title: James Meredith at Ole Miss
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Air Force veteran, after a year of legal battles, became the first Black student to enroll at a Mississippi university with a deep segregationist tradition. His arrival on campus sparked a night-long riot by a mob of 3,000 whites that killed two people and injured hundreds. Federal marshals and troops protected him through graduation.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1962 — Oxford, Mississippi. President Kennedy sent 30,000 federal troops, the largest domestic military deployment since the Civil War. Governor Ross Barnett had personally tried to block Meredith four times. Meredith graduated with a degree in political science.

events.title: Los Angeles Riots
events.blurb: Four police officers filmed beating a Black motorist named Rodney King for 81 seconds after a traffic chase were acquitted of assault by a jury with no Black members. Within hours, six days of rioting erupted across South Central Los Angeles. 63 people died, 2,383 were injured, and $1 billion in property damage was inflicted — making it the costliest civil disturbance in U.S. history.
events.revealBlurb: April 29 to May 4, 1992. King himself pleaded: "Can we all get along?" The officers were subsequently retried on federal civil rights charges; two were convicted. Korean-owned small businesses in "Koreatown" were disproportionately destroyed and inadequately protected.

events.title: Explorer 1 — First US Satellite
events.blurb: A Juno I rocket launched the United States' first satellite from Cape Canaveral, placing an 8.3 kg cylinder into an elliptical orbit that reached 2,550 km altitude. The satellite's Geiger–Müller tube detected a region of intense radiation surrounding Earth — data that led James Van Allen to identify the radiation belts bearing his name.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1958 — Explorer 1. The US had been beaten to orbit by Sputnik 1 and Sputnik 2 in the previous three months. In a press conference photo, three scientists hoisted a full-scale model over their heads in triumph — the actual satellite weighed less than a toaster oven. Explorer 1 remained in orbit for 12 years.

events.title: First Soft Moon Landing
events.blurb: The Soviet Luna 9 spacecraft landed intact on the Ocean of Storms, becoming the first vehicle to achieve a controlled soft landing on another world and transmit photographs from the surface. Its four petal-shaped panels opened to right the lander and deploy an antenna, then it sent back a panoramic image sequence over three sessions totaling nine images.
events.revealBlurb: February 3, 1966 — Luna 9. British radio astronomers at Jodrell Bank intercepted the transmission and noticed it used the same format as a standard wire-photo machine. They borrowed a Müller facsimile unit from a news agency and published the images before the Soviets released them officially — to Moscow's considerable irritation.

events.title: First Crewed Lunar Orbit
events.blurb: Three astronauts fired their Service Propulsion System engine on Christmas Eve to enter orbit 112 km above the Moon — the first humans to leave Earth's gravitational sphere of influence and orbit another world. During the mission's ninth orbit, Bill Anders photographed a crescent Earth rising over the lunar horizon, producing what became one of the most widely reproduced photographs in history.
events.revealBlurb: December 24, 1968 — Apollo 8. An estimated one billion people across 64 countries watched the Christmas Eve television broadcast in which the crew read the opening verses of Genesis. The Earthrise photograph is credited with catalyzing the environmental movement; the image appeared on the first Earth Day poster in 1970.

events.title: Columbia Reentry Breakup
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated over Texas and Louisiana during reentry, killing all seven crew members 16 minutes before its scheduled landing. A 1.2 kg piece of insulating foam had struck the leading edge of the left wing at liftoff 16 days earlier, breaching a reinforced carbon-carbon thermal protection panel and allowing superheated plasma to enter the wing structure during descent.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 2003 — STS-107. Columbia was the oldest shuttle in the fleet, on its 28th mission. Debris was recovered across 2,000 km of Texas and Louisiana; some experiments in sealed canisters survived, including a container of worms (C. elegans) that lived through the breakup. It was the second shuttle lost in 113 flights.

events.title: First Orbital Rocket Booster Landing
events.blurb: A SpaceX Falcon 9 first stage returned from an orbital-class mission and landed upright at Landing Zone 1 in Cape Canaveral, completing the first successful recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster under propulsive control. The same vehicle had delivered 11 commercial satellites to orbit minutes earlier and touched down within about 10 meters of the target pad.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2015 — OG-2 Mission 2. SpaceX had attempted and failed four previous booster landings on a drone ship at sea. The Falcon's legs deployed at 180 m altitude. Elon Musk posted one word after confirmation: "Welcome back, baby." The reused booster concept cut launch costs by roughly 30%.

events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years. The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Hundred Years' War Begins
events.blurb: An English king, claiming the French throne through his mother on the extinction of the main French royal line, formally renounced his homage for his continental territories and declared himself the rightful king of France. The resulting dynastic war would last 116 years across five generations, introduce the longbow as a battlefield weapon, and eventually produce the nation-states of France and England.
events.revealBlurb: 1337 — Edward III vs. Philip VI. The conflict ran in spasms with long truces, and is named "Hundred Years" only in retrospect. Joan of Arc arrived in its fifth generation; gunpowder arrived in its fourth.

events.title: Battle of Crécy
