events.blurb: An outnumbered English army of longbowmen and dismounted knights, arrayed behind earthworks on a hillside in northern France, destroyed a confident French chivalric force that charged uphill through their own crossbowmen. The battle demonstrated that skilled commoner archers could annihilate mounted aristocracy, and it made the English longbow the most feared weapon in Europe for the next seventy years.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1346 — Edward III and the Black Prince, early Hundred Years' War. The blind king of Bohemia, fighting on the French side, asked his knights to tie his horse to theirs so he could strike one blow. They did; he did; they all died together.

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.blurb: An Ottoman sultan, 21 years old, directed a 53-day siege of the Byzantine capital with 80,000 troops, an army of miners who tunneled under the walls, and enormous bronze cannons that fired 550-kilogram stone balls. The last Roman emperor died fighting at a breach in his city's walls. The 1,100-year-old Byzantine state, the direct legal continuation of Roman rule, ended.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1453 — Mehmed II. The city's Greek name, Constantinople, stayed in formal Ottoman use until 1930; "Istanbul" is how Byzantine Greeks had always said "to the city" colloquially. Hagia Sophia became a mosque that Friday.

events.title: Chauvet Cave Paintings
events.blurb: Deep inside a limestone gorge in southern France, artists of the Upper Paleolithic ventured hundreds of metres into darkness with torches of burning pine and painted more than 400 animals onto the walls — rhinos, horses, cave lions, mammoths — using charcoal and red ochre. The images show sophisticated techniques: perspective, shading, motion. They would remain sealed behind a rockslide until rediscovered by three cavers in 1994.
events.revealBlurb: c. 30,000 BCE — Chauvet-Pont-d'Arc, Ardèche. Radiocarbon dating of the charcoal remains controversial; estimates span 32,000-30,000 BCE. A meticulous replica opened to tourists in 2015; the original site is restricted to scientists to preserve a fragile microclimate.

events.title: Caravaggio's Calling of St Matthew
events.blurb: A 28-year-old painter completed the first of three monumental canvases for a chapel in a Roman church, depicting the moment when Christ walks into a tax collector's office and wordlessly summons a clerk to follow him. A shaft of natural light cuts diagonally across the scene, picking out faces from deep shadow. The painter used Roman street-people as models and dressed the apostles in contemporary clothes. The effect shocked and recruited a generation of imitators across Europe.
events.revealBlurb: 1600 — Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio, at the Contarelli Chapel, San Luigi dei Francesi. Art historians still argue about which figure is Matthew. The painter killed a man in a brawl six years later and died on the run at 38.

events.title: Van Gogh Cuts Off His Ear
events.blurb: After a violent argument with a fellow painter who had been living with him at a small yellow house in Provence for nine weeks, a 35-year-old Dutch artist cut off part of his own left ear with a razor, wrapped it in newspaper, and walked through the rain to deliver the package to a woman at a nearby brothel. He spent the night lying in a pool of blood. The fellow painter left the next morning. The injured man was committed to an asylum.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1888 — Vincent van Gogh; the houseguest was Paul Gauguin. He painted "Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear" within weeks. He sold only one painting in his lifetime and shot himself 19 months later in a Paris suburb.

events.title: Van Gogh Paints The Starry Night
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Dutch painter, voluntarily committed to a mental asylum in a Provençal town, painted from memory — and through the bars of his east-facing window — a night sky filled with swirling nebulae and stars dozens of times their actual size, above a village with an exaggeratedly prominent church steeple. He considered the painting a failure. It is now among the most recognized images in Western art.
events.revealBlurb: June 1889 — Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum, Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. The village in the picture does not match the actual view. The Museum of Modern Art in New York has owned it since 1941. Recent research suggests the sky's swirls resemble actual fluid turbulence.

events.title: Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans
events.blurb: A 33-year-old former commercial illustrator exhibited 32 canvases, each showing a single can of condensed soup — one for each of the 32 varieties the food company then sold. He had painted them by projecting photographic images onto the canvas and tracing. The show sold modestly: five of the canvases went for $100 each; the gallery owner bought them back and later resold the whole set for $2 million.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1962 — Ferus Gallery, Los Angeles, Andy Warhol. The artist said he ate Campbell's soup every day for 20 years. The set is now in MoMA. Warhol would soon apply the same silk-screen methods to Marilyn Monroe, Jackie Kennedy, and Elvis.

events.title: U-2 Incident
events.blurb: A high-altitude American reconnaissance aircraft was shot down deep inside Soviet territory by a surface-to-air missile. The CIA assumed the pilot was dead and issued a cover story about a weather research flight gone astray. Then Khrushchev triumphantly produced the pilot alive and the wreckage intact, humiliating the U.S. president on the eve of a Paris summit.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1960 — pilot Francis Gary Powers ejected over Sverdlovsk (now Yekaterinburg). He was traded two years later for Soviet spy Rudolf Abel on Berlin's Glienicke Bridge — the same swap dramatized in "Bridge of Spies."

events.title: Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan
events.blurb: Thousands of Soviet paratroopers and mechanized divisions crossed into a central Asian country to prop up a failing Marxist government, assassinating the sitting president in the process and installing a more pliable replacement. The operation was supposed to last weeks. Instead it dragged on for nearly a decade, bleeding the Soviet treasury, radicalizing a generation of fighters, and helping bring the superpower down.
events.revealBlurb: December 24-27, 1979 — the intervention cost the USSR an estimated 15,000 dead and 35,000 wounded. The US, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan funneled billions in arms to the mujahideen, some of whom would later form al-Qaeda.

events.title: "Evil Empire" Speech
events.blurb: Addressing the National Association of Evangelicals in Florida, a U.S. president abandoned the detente rhetoric of his predecessors and described the rival superpower as "the focus of evil in the modern world." Speechwriters had lifted the phrase from a Star Wars reference. The framing shocked diplomats but reflected a deeper strategy: rhetorically delegitimize the opponent rather than coexist with it.
events.revealBlurb: March 8, 1983 — Ronald Reagan in Orlando. Speechwriter Tony Dolan had sneaked "evil empire" past the State Department, which had deleted it from earlier drafts. Two weeks later Reagan announced the Strategic Defense Initiative.

events.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
events.blurb: An East German spokesman, reading hastily from a note and misunderstanding its contents, announced at a televised press conference that new travel rules would take effect "immediately." Within hours, tens of thousands of jubilant East Berliners massed at the crossings. Confused border guards, receiving no clear orders, simply let them through. People scrambled onto the concrete barrier with hammers.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 1989 — the spokesman was Günter Schabowski, who had skimmed the briefing note just before the press conference. Asked when the rules took effect, he shrugged: "As far as I know — immediately." The wall, built in a single night 28 years earlier, came down in a single night too.

events.title: Romanian Revolution
events.blurb: Within ten days, a dictator who had ruled a Balkan nation for 24 years lost control of a mass demonstration, fled the capital by helicopter, was captured, given a two-hour military tribunal, and executed by firing squad on Christmas Day alongside his wife. It was the only violent collapse among the eastern bloc regimes that fell at the time.
events.revealBlurb: December 16-25, 1989 — Nicolae and Elena Ceaușescu. Soldiers actually had to be ordered to stop shooting them — they kept firing at the already-dead bodies. Ceaușescu's final request was to sing the Internationale. It was denied.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.blurb: The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the sixteen-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna — a boy whose mocking nickname meant "Little Augustus" — and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, informing the eastern emperor that the west no longer needed a separate ruler. Odoacer spared Romulus's life, finding him too young and too minor to bother executing, and exiled him to a villa in Campania on a pension.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 476 CE. The last western emperor's name combined the city's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony Roman writers noticed immediately. Contemporaries did not regard this moment as "the fall of Rome"; that framing came centuries later. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued for another 977 years.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: William the Conqueror Crowned
events.blurb: Ten weeks after winning a decisive battle on the south coast of England, the Norman duke who had invaded was crowned king at a Westminster abbey. During the coronation, Norman guards outside the abbey mistook acclamations for riot and set fire to nearby houses; the new king was hurriedly anointed while smoke drifted through the doors. He would never be popular with his new subjects.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1066 — Westminster Abbey. William spent the next two decades building castles, compiling the Domesday Book, and crushing rebellions. He was buried in Caen, and his tomb was opened, profaned, and emptied of bones during the French Revolution.

events.title: Murder of Thomas Becket
events.blurb: Four knights, prompted by an angry outburst from their king over the head of the English church, rode to a cathedral in southern England and hacked the archbishop to death in his own nave after he refused to reconsider his excommunications of clergy who had sided with the king. The murder scandalized Christendom; pilgrimages to the martyr's tomb began within weeks and continued for 368 years.
events.revealBlurb: December 29, 1170 — Canterbury Cathedral, Thomas Becket killed by four knights of Henry II. The king's supposed outburst — "Who will rid me of this turbulent priest?" — may be apocryphal. Becket was canonized within three years; T.S. Eliot turned the story into "Murder in the Cathedral."

events.title: Siege of Orléans Lifted
events.blurb: A 17-year-old peasant girl from Lorraine, dressed in white armour and claiming visions from saints, led a French relief army into a besieged Loire Valley city. Over eight days of sorties, she personally led assaults on the English siege forts around the city, was shot through the shoulder with a crossbow bolt, returned to the fight, and broke the siege. The French war effort, exhausted for a generation, was transformed overnight.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1429 — Joan of Arc relieves Orléans. She had convinced a skeptical Dauphin to give her an army by passing a theological interrogation and, reportedly, a virginity test. She would see him crowned as Charles VII at Reims within ten weeks.

events.title: Mount Tambora Eruption
events.blurb: A volcano on an Indonesian island blew its top in the most powerful eruption in recorded history, spewing 150 cubic kilometres of material into the atmosphere. The sulphate aerosols lingered in the stratosphere for years, cooling global temperatures by roughly a degree and producing crop failures, famine, and snow in June across the northern hemisphere the following year.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 1815 — Mount Tambora on Sumbawa, Indonesia. 1816 became "the year without a summer." Mary Shelley, trapped indoors by endless rain in Switzerland, wrote Frankenstein. J.M.W. Turner's lurid sunsets from the decade owe their color to Tambora's dust.

events.title: Hindenburg Disaster
events.blurb: A German passenger airship, the largest aircraft ever flown, caught fire as it approached its mooring mast at a New Jersey naval air station, and was consumed in less than 40 seconds. 36 of the 97 people on board died, along with one ground crew member. A radio reporter's anguished live commentary — "Oh, the humanity!" — entered popular idiom.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1937 — Lakehurst, NJ. The reporter was Herbert Morrison; he was actually there to record for later broadcast and didn't expect to be on air. The disaster effectively killed the commercial airship industry overnight.

events.title: Indian Ocean Tsunami
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the western coast of Sumatra — the third-largest ever recorded — displaced so much water that tsunami waves up to 30 metres high raced across the Indian Ocean, hitting 14 countries within hours. Around 228,000 people died in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and as far away as Somalia. No warning system existed.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 2004 — Boxing Day. A 10-year-old British girl named Tilly Smith recognized the receding tide from a school geography lesson and got her family's Phuket beach evacuated, saving around 100 lives. A basin-wide warning system was operational by 2006.

events.title: Haiti Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck an impoverished Caribbean nation 25 kilometres from its capital, collapsing the presidential palace, the cathedral, and roughly 250,000 homes built to no meaningful engineering standards. Estimates of the dead range from 100,000 to 316,000 — about 3 percent of the country's population. The recovery was plagued by mismanagement and a cholera outbreak accidentally introduced by UN peacekeepers.
events.revealBlurb: January 12, 2010 — Port-au-Prince. International pledges totaled $13 billion; only a fraction was ever delivered or effectively spent. An estimated 1.5 million people were displaced. Nepalese UN troops inadvertently introduced cholera that killed another 10,000+ people over the following years.

events.title: Black Summer Bushfires
events.blurb: A prolonged drought and record heat fueled a six-month season of bushfires that burned 24 million hectares of southeastern Australia — an area larger than England. 33 people died directly; several hundred more from smoke. An estimated one billion wild animals perished. Smoke drifted across the Pacific and circled the globe.
events.revealBlurb: September 2019 – March 2020 — Australia. Images of koalas drinking from cyclists' water bottles and a town sheltering under blood-red skies went viral. Firefighters came from 12 countries. The season ended just as COVID-19 lockdowns began, compounding public trauma.

events.title: Indian National Congress Founded
events.blurb: Seventy-two delegates — mostly English-educated Indian lawyers, journalists, and teachers, along with a few sympathetic Britons — met at a college in a western Indian port city for a three-day conference to petition the colonial government for greater Indian representation in its administration. The polite gathering would, over six decades, become the vehicle of a mass independence movement.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1885 — Bombay (now Mumbai). The prime mover was a retired British civil servant, Allan Octavian Hume, who believed organized political expression would prevent revolution. He was half right.

events.title: All-India Muslim League Founded
events.blurb: A group of aristocratic Muslim landowners, concerned that the Congress party would inadequately represent their community's political interests under any future system of representative government, formed a separate political organization at the close of an educational conference in a Bengali capital. It would eventually demand a separate Muslim-majority homeland, becoming the political vehicle of Pakistan.
events.revealBlurb: December 30, 1906 — Dhaka. Its initial demands were modest — reserved seats and weighted votes. Mohammad Ali Jinnah, who would lead it to the demand for Pakistan, did not even join until 1913, and left it in 1920 before returning.

events.title: Bhagat Singh Executed
events.blurb: Three young revolutionaries were hanged an hour earlier than scheduled at a jail in a Punjabi city, after a three-year trial for killing a British police officer they had mistaken for the superintendent they had meant to assassinate. The youngest of them was 23. Crowds had gathered outside the prison expecting the normal morning execution time; by the time they arrived, the bodies had already been smuggled out and cremated by the riverside.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 1931 — Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev at Lahore Central Jail. Their martyrdom made them arguably the most venerated revolutionaries of the independence movement, an icon Gandhi's non-violent path never quite matched among the young.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: 26/11 Mumbai Attacks
events.blurb: Ten men trained by a Pakistan-based militant group landed at a fishing harbour in the country's financial capital by rubber dinghy after hijacking an Indian fishing trawler at sea, and fanned out across the city to attack a railway station, a Jewish centre, a café, and two luxury hotels. The resulting sieges lasted 60 hours. 166 people died and more than 300 were wounded. Nine attackers were killed; the sole survivor was captured, tried, and hanged four years later.
events.revealBlurb: November 26-29, 2008 — Mumbai. The captured gunman, Ajmal Kasab, was hanged on November 21, 2012. The attacks were coordinated over satellite phone from Karachi; the operational planner, Sajid Mir, was finally convicted in Pakistan in 2022.

events.title: Netscape IPO
events.blurb: A 16-month-old Silicon Valley company that had distributed free web browsers and had never turned a profit went public at $28 a share, opened at $71, and closed its first trading day at $58.25. Its 24-year-old co-founder was suddenly worth $58 million on paper. Wall Street had discovered the internet, and the next five years of stock-market mania had a starting gun.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1995 — Netscape Communications. Co-founder Marc Andreessen ended up on the cover of Time two years later with the caption "The Kid Who Tamed the Web." Microsoft's bundled Internet Explorer would eventually kill Netscape; the company sold to AOL in 1999.

events.title: Y2K Rollover
events.blurb: As the world's time zones successively crossed the boundary between the 20th and 21st centuries, decades of doomsday predictions — that computer systems storing years as two digits would interpret "00" as 1900 and crash vital infrastructure — largely failed to materialize. An estimated $300 billion had been spent worldwide on remediation code. Whether the peaceful transition vindicated the expense or exposed it as overblown remains contested.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 2000 — New Zealand and Pacific islands hit midnight first, without incident. Actual bugs did occur — a French meteorological satellite briefly misreported dates, some slot machines froze, a few nuclear plants had cooling-monitor glitches — but nothing catastrophic. The fix, written in COBOL in the 1990s, may be the largest software project ever.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: Gangnam Style Hits 1 Billion Views
events.blurb: A music video by a 34-year-old South Korean rapper satirizing the upper-class culture of a Seoul neighborhood crossed a threshold no online video had previously reached, having accumulated a billion views on a major video platform in just over five months. Its horse-riding dance became a global meme and introduced a generation of Western audiences to K-pop. It broke the video platform's 32-bit view counter, forcing an engineering upgrade.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2012 — PSY's "Gangnam Style." It held the title of most-viewed YouTube video for five years before being overtaken by "Despacito." The counter overflow bug was quietly patched in 2014 when the video hit over 2 billion views.

events.title: Snowden Leaks Begin
events.blurb: Two newspapers published articles based on documents leaked by a 29-year-old former NSA contractor, revealing that the U.S. government had been conducting bulk collection of American phone records from a major telecommunications company under a secret court order. The revelations continued for years; the leaker fled to Hong Kong and, after attempting to transit to Ecuador, spent years stranded in the transit zone of a Moscow airport.
events.revealBlurb: June 6, 2013 — Edward Snowden, via Glenn Greenwald at The Guardian and Barton Gellman at The Washington Post. Snowden received Russian citizenship in September 2022. Remains wanted on espionage charges in the U.S.

events.title: Great Pyramid of Giza Completed
events.blurb: A vast limestone monument covering 5.3 hectares and rising 146 metres — the tallest man-made structure for 3,800 years — was completed as the royal tomb of the second king of Egypt's Fourth Dynasty. It consists of 2.3 million blocks, each weighing 2.5 tonnes on average, quarried from nearby escarpments and shipped down the Nile. Some 20,000 paid labourers — not slaves, as was long assumed — built it in roughly twenty years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2560 BCE — Pharaoh Khufu (Cheops). It was originally clad in smooth white limestone, robbed mostly in medieval times for Cairo construction. Its internal geometry — chambers, passages, "air shafts" — continues to attract theorizing. It is the last surviving "Seven Wonders of the Ancient World."

events.title: US Capitol Cornerstone Laid
events.blurb: The president of the newly independent United States — wearing a Masonic apron — laid the cornerstone of a new federal capitol building on a wooded hill above the banks of the Potomac River. The building was meant to house the U.S. Congress. The winning design, by a Scottish-trained amateur architect, was a neoclassical rotunda crowned with a low dome; later architects would replace the dome with a much taller cast-iron one during the Civil War.
events.revealBlurb: September 18, 1793 — George Washington at Jenkins Hill (now Capitol Hill), Washington, D.C. Designer: William Thornton. The current wedding-cake dome was built 1855-1866 by Thomas U. Walter and crowned with the Statue of Freedom during the Civil War. Slave labour built much of the original building.

events.title: Brooklyn Bridge Opens
events.blurb: The longest suspension bridge in the world — 486 metres between its Gothic granite towers — opened to foot and carriage traffic linking Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Its construction had taken 14 years and cost 27 lives. The chief engineer had been paralyzed by decompression sickness while supervising caisson work; his wife Emily had effectively managed the final decade of the project from notes dictated in his sickroom.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1883 — designed by John A. Roebling (who died from a dockside accident early in construction). His son Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease and was bedridden; daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling led onsite engineering management. She was the first person to cross the completed bridge, in a carriage carrying a rooster.

events.title: Chrysler Building Completed
events.blurb: A 319-metre Manhattan skyscraper, topped with a radiator-cap-inspired sunburst spire, opened at the corner of 42nd Street and Lexington Avenue as the tallest building in the world. Its automotive-magnate patron had kept the spire a construction secret; it was assembled inside the tower's upper levels and then hoisted into place in 90 minutes, triumphing over a rival bank project down Wall Street that had briefly claimed the height title. The Empire State Building eclipsed it 11 months later.
events.revealBlurb: May 27, 1930 — architect William Van Alen for Walter Chrysler. The Art Deco ornamentation includes eagle gargoyles at the 61st floor and a 1,700-square-metre ceiling mural in the lobby. Van Alen was never paid his fee — Chrysler accused him of taking bribes from suppliers.

events.title: Burj Khalifa Opens
events.blurb: A 828-metre tapering skyscraper — Y-shaped in plan, with a buttressed central core — opened in a Gulf financial center as the tallest building in the world, dramatically taller than the previous record holder. Its construction had begun at the height of a regional real-estate bubble; by opening it had lost over 60 percent of its value and been taken over by a neighbouring emirate, after whose ruler the tower was hastily renamed. Its name had been "Burj Dubai" during construction.
events.revealBlurb: January 4, 2010 — architect Adrian Smith at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. The renamed "Burj Khalifa" honored Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, whose government bailed out Dubai during the financial crisis. Tom Cruise dangled from the outside in "Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol" (2011).

events.title: First World Series
events.blurb: A best-of-nine championship series between the American League and National League pennant winners was played — the first time the two major leagues had agreed to a postseason championship after years of cold war. An underdog American League team, the Boston Americans, defeated the heavily favoured Pittsburgh Pirates 5 games to 3. The Pirates' owner, Barney Dreyfuss, had proposed the series himself.
events.revealBlurb: October 1-13, 1903 — Boston Americans (later the Red Sox) beat the Pittsburgh Pirates. Cy Young, Boston's 36-year-old ace, started game 3 but was the losing pitcher. Dreyfuss gave his losing Pirates a share of the winners' purse to compensate. No World Series was held in 1904; it became annual from 1905.

events.title: Babe Ruth Sold to Yankees
events.blurb: A Boston baseball team's owner, needing cash to finance a Broadway musical he had invested in, sold the star pitcher and outfielder of his defending World Series champion team to the rival New York franchise for $100,000 cash plus a $300,000 loan secured by the team's stadium. The deal shipped the best player in baseball to the Yankees; Boston did not win another World Series for 86 years. Yankee championships followed in a cascade.
events.revealBlurb: January 3, 1920 — Red Sox owner Harry Frazee sold Ruth to the Yankees. The musical was "No, No, Nanette" (1925); its eventual success does not redeem the sale. Ruth would hit 714 career home runs, lead the Yankees to 7 pennants, and define American sport for a generation.

events.title: Michael Jordan's Last Shot
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Chicago Bulls star took a jump shot from the top of the key with 5.2 seconds remaining in game 6 of an NBA Finals, giving his team an 87-86 lead over the Utah Jazz in a Salt Lake City arena. Jordan's defender had slipped; the shot rattled home. The Jazz could not tie; the Bulls clinched their sixth championship in eight years. It was the last shot Jordan would take as a Chicago Bull; within weeks the team would break up and he would retire for the second time.
events.revealBlurb: June 14, 1998 — Michael Jordan's "Last Shot" over Bryon Russell. He scored the Bulls' final 8 points of the game. The 1997-98 team was documented in ESPN's 2020 "The Last Dance," which drew enormous audiences during the COVID pandemic lockdown.

events.title: Phelps Wins 8 Golds in Beijing
events.blurb: A 23-year-old American swimmer won his eighth gold medal of a single Summer Olympic Games — surpassing Mark Spitz's 36-year-old record for most golds in a single Olympics. He set or broke world records in seven of the events. His final gold came in the 4x100m medley relay. Over four Olympic Games he would win a career total of 23 golds and 28 total medals, more than any athlete in any sport before him.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 2008 — Michael Phelps at the Beijing Olympics. Spitz's previous record was 7 golds from 1972 Munich. Phelps's career gold total eventually reached 23; he retired after Rio 2016. Spitz had been a rumored spectator at many of Phelps's events.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: British Surrender at Saratoga
events.blurb: A British army of 6,000 men under a genteel general who had marched south from Canada intending to split the American colonies along the Hudson Valley found itself encircled at a rural New York hamlet after two pitched battles and dwindling supplies. The general surrendered his entire force to the American commander. It was the most consequential Allied success of the war; France, which had been secretly aiding the colonies, publicly entered the conflict four months later.
events.revealBlurb: October 17, 1777 — British general John Burgoyne surrenders to American general Horatio Gates. Burgoyne had been marching from Canada; a complementary British push up the Hudson from New York had been misdirected to Pennsylvania. The victory secured French diplomatic recognition and military alliance.

events.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man
events.blurb: The French National Constituent Assembly, meeting in a recently converted royal indoor tennis court, adopted a 17-article statement of universal rights: liberty, property, security, resistance to oppression, equality before the law, presumption of innocence, freedom of speech and religion. It did not grant women the vote or abolish slavery; revolutionaries would debate those extensions for years. It was still the most sweeping such declaration any European state had ever adopted.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1789 — a central drafter was the Marquis de Lafayette, the American Revolution veteran. The declaration was explicitly modeled on the U.S. Declaration of Independence; in fact, Jefferson, then in Paris as American minister, advised on its drafting. It remains part of France's constitutional law.

events.title: Louisiana Purchase Treaty Signed
events.blurb: American negotiators in Paris signed a treaty acquiring roughly 828,000 square miles of territory from France — doubling the size of the United States — for approximately $15 million, or about three cents per acre. The purchase, which Napoleon offered because he needed cash for his European wars, encompassed all or part of fifteen future states and opened the continent to westward expansion.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1803 — Paris. Jefferson had only authorized $10 million and was seeking to buy New Orleans alone; Napoleon offered the entire territory. Jefferson privately wondered whether he had constitutional authority to make the deal at all, but bought it anyway. The full price, with interest, came to about $23 million.

events.title: Haiti Declares Independence
events.blurb: A former slave turned general, addressing a small crowd at a town on a Caribbean island, declared the independence of a new sovereign state that replaced a French sugar colony. It took the name of the original Taíno indigenous word for the island. It was the first independent state in Latin America, the only one to emerge from a successful slave revolt, and the second republic in the Western hemisphere. European powers reacted with diplomatic ostracism; the United States refused recognition for 58 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1804 — Jean-Jacques Dessalines at Gonaïves, Haiti. France demanded reparations for "lost property" — 150 million francs — that Haiti finished paying only in 1947. The combination of debt, ostracism, and internal strife has shaped Haitian poverty for two centuries.
